IMPORTANT — WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS AND IS NOT

This manual is a personal educational reference and operating runbook. It documents your own chosen trading rules and explains how the software works. It is not personalised investment advice, and the author is not a licensed financial adviser. No setup, indicator or rule in this manual guarantees a profitable outcome. Paper-trading results do not predict live results. You are responsible for every trade you place.

HOW TO READ “VERIFY” FLAGS

Software changes. Wherever the official documentation did not confirm an exact menu name, field, default or behaviour, this manual says so with a VERIFY box instead of guessing. Before relying on any flagged item, check it in your own TrendSpider / SignalStack / Alpaca account and record what you find in the Change Log.

How to Use This Manual

Who this is for

You are intelligent and analytical, but new to day trading and new to TrendSpider. This manual therefore never assumes you know a term because it appeared earlier. Key terms are re-explained where they matter, and every term is in the Glossary (Appendix A).

The teaching pattern

Most concepts follow the same seven-step sequence:

Step Question it answers
1. Plain English What is it, in everyday words?
2. Technical definition What is it precisely (formula, rule)?
3. Visual intuition What does it look like on a chart?
4. Numerical example What do real numbers look like?
5. How I use it Where does it appear in my v1 system?
6. Common mistake What do beginners get wrong?
7. When NOT to use it When is it misleading or irrelevant?

Recommended learning sequence

Level Topic Chapters Goal before moving on
Level 1 Market basics 1 You can explain bid/ask/spread, long vs short, and each order type without notes.
Level 2 Candles 2 You can read OHLC from any candle and say what “1 candle ago” means on any timeframe.
Level 3 Indicators 3–9 You can explain VWAP, EMA9/20, RSI14, RVOL, ATR and why the 15-minute chart confirms the 5-minute chart.
Level 4 My strategy 10–22 You can recite the v1 scanner, alert, entry, stop, size, target and exit rules for LONG and SHORT.
Level 5 TrendSpider 23–31 You can build the chart, scanners, watchlists and alerts from scratch.
Level 6 Paper execution 32–37 You can place a correctly sized paper bracket-style order in under 60 seconds.
Level 7 Performance evaluation 38–40 You keep a journal and can calculate expectancy, profit factor and drawdown.

After Level 7, use Part VIII (FAQ, Troubleshooting, Cheat Sheets) as day-to-day reference, and Chapter 44 (Am I Ready for Live Trading?) as the gate before risking real money.

Conventions and box types

DEFINITION — a term explained in plain English and then technically.

WHY IT MATTERS — the practical consequence for your P/L or risk.

COMMON MISTAKE — a typical beginner error and how to avoid it.

MY v1 RULE — a rule you have chosen. These are documented exactly as you specified. They are trading decisions, not software features or universal truths.

TRENDSPIDER STEP — an instruction inside TrendSpider (or SignalStack / Alpaca), tied to official documentation where possible.

RECOMMENDATION — the author’s suggestion. Not part of v1 unless you adopt it and record the change in the Change Log.

VERIFY — something the official documentation did not confirm, or that may have changed.

[SCREENSHOT REQUIRED — SS-00 · Example placeholder] — describes exactly which screen to capture, what to crop and what to number. Replace the placeholder with your own capture; the full list is in Appendix C.

Source labels

Every factual claim falls into one of six categories. When it is not obvious from context, the text labels it:

Label Meaning
[TS] TrendSpider officially documents this.
[SS] SignalStack officially documents this.
[ALP] Alpaca officially documents this.
[REG] Regulation / exchange rule (SEC, FINRA, exchanges).
[RULE] Your chosen v1 trading rule.
[IND] General industry practice or standard indicator mathematics.
[REC] The author’s recommendation.

Number formatting

  • Prices are in US dollars, rounded to cents ($100.25).
  • “Shares” are always whole shares, rounded down.
  • Times are US Eastern Time (ET). TrendSpider states that its notifications are delivered in Eastern time [TS].
  • “5m” = 5-minute chart; “15m” = 15-minute chart; “D” = daily chart.

The Five Distinctions This Manual Repeats

These five ideas prevent most beginner disasters. They appear again throughout the manual.

# Distinction In one sentence
1 Scanner ≠ Alert A scanner finds candidates across many symbols at the moment you run it; an alert watches one symbol and notifies you when a defined setup occurs.
2 Alert ≠ Trade An alert means “go and inspect this chart”. It never means “buy now”.
3 Setup ≠ Outcome A perfect-looking setup can still lose. You are trading probabilities, not certainties.
4 Paper ≠ Live Paper fills are simulated: no market impact, no queue position, and different emotions. Paper results are an approximation.
5 Risk management > Prediction You cannot control whether a trade wins. You can always control how much it can lose.

PART I — MARKET BASICS (LEVEL 1)

1 How Day Trading Actually Works

Before looking at a single indicator, you need to know what actually happens when you click “Buy”. This chapter covers the mechanics. Everything later in the manual is built on these definitions.

1.1 Stocks and shares

DEFINITION — Stock / Share

Plain English: A stock is part-ownership of a company. A share is one unit of that ownership. Owning 100 shares of AAPL means you own 100 units of Apple Inc.

Technical: A share is an equity security that trades on an exchange (NYSE, Nasdaq) or an alternative trading venue. Its price is set by the most recent trades between buyers and sellers.

How I use it: You trade shares of S&P 500 companies priced between $10 and $500 [RULE].

Day trading means opening and closing a position within the same trading day, so that you hold nothing overnight. Your v1 system is intraday only. Every position is intended to close before the 4:00 PM ET close.

1.2 The quote: bid, ask, spread and last

At any moment there are two prices for a stock, not one.

Term Plain English Technical
Bid The highest price someone is currently willing to pay. Best (highest) buy limit order displayed. You sell at the bid if you sell immediately.
Ask (offer) The lowest price someone is currently willing to sell at. Best (lowest) sell limit order displayed. You buy at the ask if you buy immediately.
Spread The gap between them. Spread = Ask − Bid.
Last (last price) The price of the most recent trade. Last executed print. It can be at the bid, at the ask or between them.
NBBO National Best Bid and Offer. The best bid and best ask across all US exchanges.

Numerical example. A stock shows Bid $100.00 × 300, Ask $100.03 × 500, Last $100.02.

  • Spread = $100.03 − $100.00 = $0.03 (3 cents).
  • If you buy with a market order right now, you probably pay about $100.03 (the ask), not $100.02 (the last trade).
  • If you then immediately sell with a market order, you get about $100.00 (the bid).
  • Round-trip cost from the spread alone: $0.03 per share. For 500 shares that is $15, before any price movement.
  • “× 300” and “× 500” are the share quantities displayed at those prices (the size).

WHY IT MATTERS

Your v1 stop distances can be as small as $0.20–$0.50. A $0.03 spread is then 6–15% of your entire risk budget per share, paid before the trade has done anything. Wide spreads quietly destroy small-stop strategies. This is one reason the v1 universe is liquid S&P 500 stocks with more than 1M shares of average daily volume.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating “Last” as the price you will get. In a fast market, the last trade may be several cents away from where you can actually buy or sell right now.

1.3 Trading sessions

Session Time (ET) Notes
Pre-market 04:00 – 09:30 Thinner liquidity, wider spreads. Brokers usually accept only limit orders here. Alpaca: extended-hours orders must be limit with TIF day or gtc [ALP].
Regular market hours 09:30 – 16:00 Highest liquidity. v1 trades only in this session [RULE].
After-hours (post-market) 16:00 – 20:00 Thin liquidity. Earnings releases often happen here.
Alpaca overnight 20:00 – 04:00 (Sun–Fri) Alpaca documents an overnight session [ALP]. Not used in v1.

TrendSpider uses the same pre-market (04:00–09:30) and post-market (16:00–20:00) definitions for extended-hours alerts [TS].

“Market closed” in a platform means the regular session is not running. Depending on settings, quotes may still move in extended hours. A market order placed while the market is closed is either rejected or queued for the next open, which is broker-dependent. Do not do it in v1.

1.4 Order types

An order is an instruction to your broker. The order type controls price certainty versus fill certainty. You can rarely have both.

Order Plain English Fill certainty Price certainty Typical use in v1
Market “Fill me now at whatever the best available price is.” High Low (slippage) Emergency exits; possibly entries in very liquid names.
Limit “Fill me only at this price or better.” Low (may never fill) High Controlled entries; profit targets.
Stop (stop-market) “When price reaches X, send a market order.” High once triggered Low (can gap through) Stop-losses, and breakout entries (buy-stop above the signal high).
Stop-limit “When price reaches X, send a limit order at Y.” Lower (can skip past Y) Higher Breakout entries with a price cap. Not available in the TrendSpider Trading widget per its documentation [TS].
Bracket Entry plus an attached stop-loss and take-profit. When one exit fills, the other cancels. — — The ideal v1 structure. Alpaca supports it via API [ALP].
OCO “One-Cancels-Other”: two exit orders, and if one fills the other is cancelled. — — Adding stop and target to an existing position. Alpaca supports it [ALP].

1.4.1 Worked examples of each order type (LONG side)

Stock XYZ: Bid $50.00 / Ask $50.02.

  1. Market buy 100. Fills immediately at about $50.02, or worse if the ask is thin and moves up.
  2. Limit buy 100 @ $49.95. Fills only if a seller accepts $49.95 or less. If price rises, you never fill.
  3. Buy-stop 100 @ $50.30. Nothing happens until price trades at $50.30. Then a market order is sent, which might fill at $50.31–$50.35 in a fast move. This is how “buy the break of the signal candle high” works.
  4. Buy stop-limit 100, stop $50.30, limit $50.40. At $50.30 a limit order to buy at up to $50.40 is sent. If price jumps straight to $50.45, you do not fill. That protects you from a terrible price, but you miss the trade.
  5. Sell-stop 100 @ $49.70 (stop-loss on a long). If price falls to $49.70, a market sell is sent. In a gap or flash drop the fill could be $49.60 or worse.

1.4.2 Worked examples (SHORT side)

  1. Sell-short stop @ $49.70. Triggers a market short sale when price falls to $49.70. This is the mirror of a breakout entry, used for a breakdown entry.
  2. Buy-stop @ $50.30 (stop-loss on a short). If price rises to $50.30, a market buy is sent to cover (close) the short.

COMMON MISTAKE

Thinking a stop-loss guarantees the stop price. A stop guarantees only that an order is triggered at that price. The fill can be worse. That difference is slippage.

1.5 Liquidity, volume, volatility and slippage

Term Plain English Technical Why you care
Liquidity How easily you can trade without moving the price. Depth of resting orders near the NBBO, combined with tight spreads. Liquid stocks fill near your intended price.
Volume How many shares traded. Shares exchanged during a period (per candle, per day). High volume generally means more participation and liquidity.
Average volume Typical volume. Mean of daily volume over N days (v1: 20-day). v1 requires a daily volume 20-period moving average above 1,000,000 shares [RULE].
Volatility How much price moves. Dispersion of returns, often measured by ATR or standard deviation. Sets how wide stops must be and how fast P/L swings.
Slippage Getting a worse price than you planned. Fill price − intended price (long), or intended − fill (short). Turns a planned −1R loss into −1.1R or −1.3R.

Slippage example. You plan to buy 500 shares at $100.21. Your stop-entry triggers and fills at $100.26. Slippage = $0.05 × 500 = $25. If your planned risk was $250, slippage has already used 10% of it.

1.6 LONG and SHORT, explained carefully

This is the most important idea in Part I.

DEFINITION — LONG

Plain English: You buy first and sell later. You make money if price rises.

Technical: A long position is a positive share quantity. P/L = (Exit price − Entry price) × Shares.

DEFINITION — SHORT

Plain English: You sell first and buy back later. You borrow shares you don’t own, sell them now, and later buy them back (cover) to return them. You make money if price falls.

Technical: A short position is a negative share quantity. P/L = (Entry price − Exit price) × Shares. The broker must be able to locate shares to borrow (Reg SHO), and the account must be margin-enabled.

1.6.1 Long examples

# Action Entry Exit Shares P/L calculation Result
L1 Buy, price rises $100.00 $103.00 100 (103 − 100) × 100 +$300
L2 Buy, price falls $100.00 $98.00 100 (98 − 100) × 100 −$200
L3 Buy, small move $45.20 $45.65 500 (45.65 − 45.20) × 500 +$225

1.6.2 Short examples

# Action Entry (sell) Exit (buy to cover) Shares P/L calculation Result
S1 Short, price falls $100.00 $97.00 100 (100 − 97) × 100 +$300
S2 Short, price rises $100.00 $102.00 100 (100 − 102) × 100 −$200
S3 Short, small move $45.20 $44.80 500 (45.20 − 44.80) × 500 +$200

1.6.3 Short-selling step by step (S1)

  1. You sell short 100 shares at $100. Your broker borrows 100 shares for you and sells them. Your account shows −100 shares and you receive $10,000 in proceeds, which are restricted as collateral.
  2. Price falls to $97.
  3. You buy to cover 100 shares at $97, paying $9,700. The shares are returned to the lender.
  4. Profit = $10,000 − $9,700 = $300, before borrow fees and commissions.

WHY IT MATTERS — the asymmetry of short risk

A long position can lose at most 100% (price falls to $0). A short position has theoretically unlimited loss, because price can keep rising. That is why a hard stop is non-negotiable on shorts, and why gap risk (Chapter 18) matters more for shorts. In v1 every position closes intraday, which removes overnight gap risk. It does not remove halts or news spikes.

1.6.4 Regulatory realities of shorting [REG]

Rule What it says (simplified) Effect on you
Locate (Reg SHO) Brokers must have reasonable grounds to believe shares can be borrowed before a short sale. Hard-to-borrow stocks may be un-shortable. S&P 500 names are usually easy to borrow, but not always.
Short Sale Restriction / SSR (Rule 201) If a stock falls 10% or more from the prior day’s close, short sales are restricted to prices above the national best bid for the rest of that day and the next day. Your short-entry stop orders may not execute normally on SSR stocks. v1 recommendation: skip shorts on SSR-flagged stocks [REC].
Margin Shorting requires a margin account. Alpaca documents shorting support in both paper and live accounts [ALP]. Its buying-power check for an opening short uses the higher of the limit price or 3% above the ask, × quantity [ALP].

1.7 Account terms

Term Plain English Technical / Example
Cash Money not invested. Can be negative on margin accounts after buying more than your cash.
Equity / Portfolio value What the account is worth right now. Cash + market value of longs − market value of shorts. Paper account starts near $100,000.
Buying power How much stock you are allowed to buy right now. Depends on equity and margin rules. It can be 2× (overnight) or more (intraday) of equity in margin accounts. Buying power is a limit, not a target.
Position What you currently hold in one symbol. +300 AAPL (long) or −200 MSFT (short).
Realized P/L Profit/loss that is locked in because the position is closed. Bought 100 at $50, sold 100 at $51 → realized +$100.
Unrealized P/L Paper gain/loss on positions still open. Bought 100 at $50, price now $50.40 → unrealized +$40. It can disappear.

Worked equity example. Start: cash $100,000. Buy 400 shares at $50 (cost $20,000). Cash = $80,000; position value = $20,000; equity = $100,000. Price rises to $50.75: position value = $20,300; unrealized P/L = +$300; equity = $100,300. Sell all at $50.75: cash = $100,300; realized P/L = +$300; unrealized = $0.

1.7.1 The PDT rule — an important 2026 change [REG]

Until mid-2026, FINRA’s “Pattern Day Trader” rule required $25,000 minimum equity in margin accounts that made 4 or more day trades in 5 business days. The SEC approved FINRA’s amendments to Rule 4210 in April 2026, effective June 4, 2026. They remove the PDT designation and the $25,000 minimum, and replace them with an intraday margin standard for all margin customers. Brokers may phase this in until October 20, 2027. Alpaca announced implementation on June 4, 2026 and deprecation of its PDT API fields [ALP].

VERIFY

Alpaca’s “User Protection” page still described the old PDT protection when checked on 2026-10-28, while its changelog and forum describe the change. Confirm in your Alpaca dashboard whether your paper account still applies any day-trade-count protection. This matters mostly when you later trade a live account below $25,000.

1.8 Anatomy of a trade

Term Plain English Example (LONG) Example (SHORT)
Entry Price at which you open. Buy at $100.25 Sell short at $99.75
Stop-loss Pre-set price where you admit you are wrong and exit. Sell-stop at $99.75 Buy-stop at $100.25
Take-profit (target) Pre-set price where you take the gain. Sell limit at $101.25 Buy limit at $98.75
Exit Price at which you close, for any reason. — —
Risk/share What you lose per share if stopped. 100.25 − 99.75 = $0.50 100.25 − 99.75 = $0.50
Reward/share What you gain per share at target. 101.25 − 100.25 = $1.00 99.75 − 98.75 = $1.00
Risk/reward (R:R) Reward ÷ risk. 1.00 / 0.50 = 2:1 (2R) 2:1 (2R)

1.9 Market structure vocabulary

Term Plain English How it looks How v1 uses it
Support A price zone where buying has repeatedly stopped declines. Multiple lows near the same level. A short entry just above major support is poor: little room to fall.
Resistance A zone where selling has repeatedly stopped advances. Multiple highs near the same level. A long entry just below major resistance is poor.
Breakout Price moves above resistance with conviction. Strong candle closing above a level, ideally on high volume. LONG entry = break of the signal candle high (a micro-breakout).
Breakdown Price moves below support. Strong candle closing below a level. SHORT entry = break of the signal candle low.
Pullback A temporary move against the trend. Uptrend dips toward VWAP/EMA20, then resumes. Often a better-priced entry than chasing.
Retest Price returns to a broken level to “test” it from the other side. Old resistance acts as new support. Confirmation that a breakout is real.
Trend Persistent direction. Higher highs and higher lows (up); lower highs and lower lows (down). EMA9 vs EMA20, VWAP and the 15m EMA20 define trend in v1.
Consolidation Sideways, range-bound trading. Overlapping candles, flat EMAs. Signals fail more often here.
Momentum Speed and persistence of a move. Large candles in one direction, rising RSI. v1 is a momentum system.
Reversal Trend changes direction. Lower high after an uptrend, VWAP lost, EMAs cross. Reversals trigger v1 Exit C (trend failure).
Gap Open far from the prior close, with an empty space on the chart. Daily open 3% above yesterday’s close. Large gaps distort early indicators; see the “extreme gap” checklist item.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating support and resistance as exact lines. They are zones. A level at $150.00 may “hold” at $149.85 or $150.20.

PART II — CANDLES (LEVEL 2)

2 Candlesticks — Complete Beginner Training

THE ONE RULE OF THIS CHAPTER

Never trade a candlestick pattern in isolation. Context matters. In v1, a candle is meaningful only inside the full checklist: VWAP, EMA alignment, RSI, RVOL and 15-minute confirmation.

2.1 The four prices: Open, High, Low, Close (OHLC)

Plain English: A candle summarises everything that happened during one fixed slice of time.

Price Meaning
Open (O) First traded price of the period.
High (H) Highest traded price of the period.
Low (L) Lowest traded price of the period.
Close (C) Last traded price of the period. For a candle still forming, the “close” is the current price and keeps changing until the period ends.
Part Definition Formula
Body Rectangle between Open and Close. Body = |Close − Open|
Upper wick (shadow) Line above the body. Upper wick = High − max(Open, Close)
Lower wick Line below the body. Lower wick = min(Open, Close) − Low
Range Full height. Range = High − Low
Bullish candle Close > Open (usually green/hollow). —
Bearish candle Close < Open (usually red/filled). —
Body % How much of the range is body. Body ÷ Range

Numerical example. O $100.00, H $101.60, L $99.40, C $101.00.

  • Body = 101.00 − 100.00 = $1.00 (bullish)
  • Upper wick = 101.60 − 101.00 = $0.60
  • Lower wick = 100.00 − 99.40 = $0.60
  • Range = 101.60 − 99.40 = $2.20
  • Body % = 1.00 / 2.20 = 45%

2.2 Candle timeframe

A candle’s timeframe is the length of time it summarises.

Timeframe One candle = Candles in a regular session (6.5 h) Typical use
1-minute 60 seconds of trading 390 Precision timing. Very noisy for beginners.
5-minute 5 minutes 78 v1 entry chart.
15-minute 15 minutes 26 v1 confirmation chart.
Daily One full trading session 1 per day Universe filters (price, average volume, daily % change).

A 5-minute candle labelled 10:00 covers 10:00:00–10:04:59 in most charting conventions (time labels mark the start of the bar). The 10:00 candle closes at 10:05.

VERIFY — bar timestamp convention

Most platforms, including TrendSpider by common convention, label bars by their open time. Confirm on your chart by hovering the first regular-session 5m bar: it should read 9:30, and its close should appear at 9:35.

2.3 What “1 candle ago” means

“N candles ago” counts bars on the condition’s own timeframe, not minutes.

Timeframe of the condition “Current candle” “1 candle ago” “3 candles ago”
5-minute The 5m bar in progress (or just closed — see below) The previous 5-minute bar 15 minutes earlier
15-minute Current 15m bar Previous 15-minute bar 45 minutes earlier
Daily Today’s session Yesterday’s session (previous trading day) 3 trading days ago; weekends and holidays are skipped

TrendSpider’s scripting uses offsets for this. A condition with no offset reads the latest value, and its help gives the example of comparing today’s close with the prior day’s close using a one-candle offset [TS]. In indicator settings, Offset 0 = current candle, −1 = previous candle, −2 = the one before [TS].

2.3.1 “Current” depends on scanner/alert settings

  • Market Scanner with Current Candle ON treats the still-forming candle as if it were closed [TS]. With it OFF, the scan uses the most recent closed candle [TS].
  • Multi-Factor Alerts are checked when the candle of the smallest timeframe in the alert closes (e.g., every 5 minutes for a 5m alert) [TS]. Your 5m conditions are therefore evaluated on a completed 5m candle. That completed candle is your signal candle.

COMMON MISTAKE

Reading “Close > Open” on a forming candle and treating it as final. A candle that is green at 10:02 can close red at 10:05.

2.4 Candle forms

For each form below: structure → what buyers/sellers did → LONG reading → SHORT reading → when meaningful → when meaningless.

2.4.1 Strong bullish candle

Aspect Description
Structure Large green body (≥ ~70% of range), small wicks, closes near the high.
Buyers/sellers Buyers controlled the whole period and were still pushing at the close.
LONG Supportive, especially when it closes above VWAP and EMA9 > EMA20. Often a v1 signal candle.
SHORT Warning: do not short into it.
Meaningful when It follows a pullback to VWAP/EMA20, on elevated RVOL, aligned with the 15m.
Meaningless/dangerous when It is 3–5× the average candle size after an extended run (exhaustion, poor stop placement), or a news spike.

2.4.2 Strong bearish candle

The exact mirror: large red body, closes near the low. Sellers controlled the period. It supports a SHORT when below VWAP with EMA9 < EMA20, and warns against a LONG. It is dangerous to short when enormous and far below VWAP (snap-back risk).

2.4.3 Doji

Aspect Description
Structure Open ≈ Close (tiny body), wicks on one or both sides.
Buyers/sellers Balance. Neither side won the period.
LONG / SHORT Indecision. Neither a buy nor a sell signal by itself.
Meaningful when It appears after a strong run at a key level, and the next candle breaks decisively.
Meaningless when It appears mid-range in quiet consolidation, which is common and carries no information.
v1 note A doji cannot satisfy “Close > Open” (or “<”) meaningfully, so v1 alerts will rarely fire on one.

2.4.4 Hammer

Aspect Description
Structure Small body near the top; lower wick ≥ 2× body; little upper wick. Colour matters less.
Buyers/sellers Sellers pushed price down hard, buyers pushed it all the way back.
LONG Potential bullish reversal after a decline into support.
SHORT Warning for shorts: buyers defended the lows.
Meaningful At support, VWAP or prior day low, after a downtrend, with volume.
Meaningless In the middle of nowhere, or in a strong downtrend without confirmation.

2.4.5 Inverted hammer

Small body near the bottom, long upper wick, after a decline. Buyers tried to push up and failed by the close, but the attempt itself can signal a shift. It needs next-candle confirmation. It is weaker than a hammer.

2.4.6 Shooting star

The same shape as an inverted hammer, but after an advance: long upper wick, small body near the low. Buyers pushed up and sellers rejected the high. It is a potential bearish reversal at resistance. It warns LONGs and supports SHORT setups with confirmation.

2.4.7 Long lower wick / long upper wick

Candle Message LONG reading SHORT reading
Long lower wick Lower prices were rejected. Supportive near support/VWAP. Caution: buyers are present.
Long upper wick Higher prices were rejected. Caution: sellers are present. Supportive near resistance/VWAP.

Numerical example (long upper wick). O $50.10, H $51.00, L $50.00, C $50.20. Upper wick = 51.00 − 50.20 = $0.80 out of a $1.00 range (80%). Price touched $51 and was sold off.

2.4.8 Bullish engulfing

Aspect Description
Structure Red candle followed by a green candle whose body fully covers the prior body.
Meaning Buyers overwhelmed the prior period’s sellers.
LONG Potential reversal or continuation trigger at support/VWAP.
SHORT Warning against shorting.
Meaningful After a pullback in an uptrend, on above-average volume.
Meaningless Small candles in chop.

2.4.9 Bearish engulfing

The mirror: a green candle followed by a red candle whose body covers it. Sellers overwhelmed buyers. It supports SHORT at resistance or below VWAP and warns LONGs.

2.4.10 Inside bar

The second candle’s high and low are both inside the prior candle’s range. It signals contraction or a pause. A break out of the inside bar’s range, in the direction of the trend, can be a trigger. Inside bars are common, so they are meaningful only at decision points.

2.4.11 Breakout candle

A candle that closes beyond a defined level (resistance, prior high, consolidation range), ideally with large volume. LONG: confirmation of a breakout. SHORT: the breakdown version closes below support. It is meaningless if it closes back inside the range (a “failed breakout”) or if the move is a single huge bar after the trend has already extended.

2.4.12 Rejection candle

A candle that trades through a level but closes back on the original side, leaving a long wick through the level. For example, price pokes above resistance at $150, hits $150.40 and closes at $149.90. It shows that the level held. It warns against a LONG breakout and supports a SHORT. The mirror at support works the other way.

2.5 Context checklist for any candle

Ask these five questions before giving any candle meaning:

  1. Where is it? At support/resistance/VWAP, or in the middle of a range?
  2. What came before? A trend, a pullback or a chop?
  3. How large is it relative to recent candles and to ATR?
  4. What was volume/RVOL? High volume gives more weight.
  5. What does the higher timeframe (15m) say?

COMMON MISTAKE

Memorising pattern names and trading every one. Studies of candlestick patterns in isolation show weak and inconsistent edges. Their value comes from location and confirmation, which is exactly what your v1 indicator stack supplies.

PART III — INDICATORS (LEVEL 3)

WHICH INDICATORS ARE IN v1?

Indicator Status Where it is used
VWAP v1 core Scanner, alert, exit C
EMA9, EMA20 (5m) v1 core Scanner, alert, exit C
EMA20 (15m) v1 core Scanner, alert (higher-timeframe confirmation)
RSI14 v1 core Scanner (>55 / <45), alert, ranking (55–70 / 30–45)
Relative Volume (RVOL20) v1 core Scanner (>2.0), alert (>1.5)
Volume / Volume MA20 (daily) v1 core Universe filter (>1M shares)
ATR v1 reference only Sanity-checks stop size and “too extended”. Not a hard rule.
SMA, MACD, Bollinger, ADX, Stochastic, RS, ADR, pivots Optional / future Not part of v1 decisions

3 VWAP — Volume Weighted Average Price

3.1 Plain English

VWAP is the average price paid for every share traded so far today, where each price is weighted by how many shares traded there. It answers: “On average, is today’s buyer in profit or in loss right now?”

3.2 Technical definition [IND]

For each candle i since the session start (standard VWAP resets at the session open):

  • Typical price (when Price Source = HLC3): TPᵢ = (Highᵢ + Lowᵢ + Closeᵢ) ÷ 3
  • VWAP = Σ(TPᵢ × Volumeᵢ) ÷ Σ Volumeᵢ

where Σ means “sum over all candles from the session start to now”, and Volumeᵢ is the shares traded in candle i.

3.3 Why volume weighting matters — numerical example

Bar High Low Close TP = (H+L+C)/3 Volume TP × Volume
1 100.50 99.50 100.20 100.0667 10,000 1,000,667
2 101.00 100.10 100.90 100.6667 30,000 3,020,000
3 101.20 100.60 100.70 100.8333 5,000 504,167
Σ 45,000 4,524,833
  • VWAP = 4,524,833 ÷ 45,000 = $100.55
  • A simple average of the three typical prices = $100.52
  • VWAP is pulled toward bar 2 because two-thirds of all shares traded there. That is where most participants have their cost basis.

3.4 How traders read VWAP

Situation Plain English LONG implication SHORT implication
Price above VWAP The average buyer today is in profit, so buyers are in control. Favourable; required by v1 Unfavourable; v1 shorts not allowed
Price below VWAP The average buyer is underwater, so sellers are in control. Unfavourable Favourable; required by v1
VWAP as support In uptrends, pullbacks often stall at VWAP. Pullback-to-VWAP entries —
VWAP as resistance In downtrends, rallies often stall at VWAP. — Rally-to-VWAP entries
VWAP reclaim Price was below, closes back above. Possible new long setup Short thesis invalidated
VWAP rejection Price pokes through VWAP but closes back on the original side. At VWAP from below: bearish From above: bullish
Distance from VWAP How stretched price is. Far above = overextended, snap-back risk Far below = overextended

3.5 Standard vs Anchored VWAP

Type Starts summing from Use
Standard (session) VWAP The session open (9:30 ET, or 4:00 ET if extended hours are included). Intraday trend reference. Institutional benchmark.
Anchored VWAP (AVWAP) A point you choose (earnings day, swing low, gap day). “Average cost since event X.” TrendSpider has a separate Anchored VWAP indicator [TS].

3.6 TrendSpider VWAP parameters — what VWAP(14, 0, HLC3) means

TrendSpider lists three VWAP inputs [TS]:

Parameter Your value TrendSpider’s documented meaning
Length 14 “Number of periods used in the calculation.”
Offset 0 Which candle the value is read from: 0 = current candle, −1 = previous, −2 = the one before.
Price Source HLC3 The candle data point used (open, high, low, close, or a combination). HLC3 = (High + Low + Close) ÷ 3, the classic VWAP “typical price”.

So VWAP(14, 0, HLC3) reads as “VWAP, length 14, current candle, typical price”.

VERIFY — what “Length 14” does to VWAP in TrendSpider

A standard session VWAP has no lookback length: it sums from the session open. TrendSpider’s VWAP help page lists Length as “number of periods” but does not say whether VWAP (a) resets each session and ignores Length, (b) is a rolling 14-bar volume-weighted average (on a 5m chart that is the last ~70 minutes), or (c) something else. These give materially different lines, especially after 11:00 ET.

Test (10 minutes, do it once):

  1. On a 5m AAPL chart, add your VWAP(14, 0, HLC3).
  2. Add a second VWAP with a very different Length (e.g., 50) and a Anchored VWAP anchored at today’s 9:30 candle.
  3. At 13:00 ET compare the three values.
    • If all three match → Length is ignored; your VWAP is a true session VWAP.
    • If the 14 and 50 versions differ → Length creates a rolling VWAP. Decide deliberately which you want (see Chapter 22, v2 item 1).
  4. Record the result in the Change Log.

Whatever the result: the chart, the scanner and the alerts must use identical VWAP settings. Otherwise a chart that “looks above VWAP” may not match the alert’s VWAP (see Troubleshooting).

3.7 How v1 uses VWAP

MY v1 RULE — VWAP

  • LONG scanner and alert: 5m Close > VWAP.
  • SHORT scanner and alert: 5m Close < VWAP.
  • Exit C (trend failure): a LONG is exited on a 5m close below VWAP, and a SHORT on a 5m close above VWAP.
  • Ranking: prefer price above but not far above VWAP (LONG); below but not far below (SHORT).

COMMON MISTAKE

Buying simply because price is above VWAP. In a strong trend price may be above VWAP all day, including at the exact top. VWAP is a filter (which side to trade), not a trigger (when to trade).

When NOT to rely on VWAP: in the first 5–15 minutes (very few bars, so VWAP is unstable); on low-volume days; across multiple days (session VWAP resets); on daily or higher timeframes.

4 Moving Averages — SMA and EMA

4.1 Simple Moving Average (SMA)

Plain English: The plain average of the last N closing prices. It smooths out noise.

Formula [IND]: SMA(N) = (C₁ + C₂ + … + C_N) ÷ N, where C₁…C_N are the last N closes.

Example: Last five 5m closes: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 → SMA5 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12. The next close is 15. Drop 10, add 15 → 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 → SMA5 = 13.

Common SMA On a daily chart On a 5m chart
SMA20 ~1 month of trading 100 minutes
SMA50 ~2.5 months ~4 hours
SMA200 ~10 months; the classic long-term trend line ~2.5 sessions

Changing the timeframe changes the meaning. “SMA20” is 20 candles, so its time span depends entirely on the timeframe.

4.2 Exponential Moving Average (EMA)

Plain English: A moving average that gives more weight to recent candles, so it reacts faster than an SMA.

Formula [IND]:

  • α (smoothing factor) = 2 ÷ (N + 1)
  • EMA_today = α × Close_today + (1 − α) × EMA_yesterday
EMA α Weight on newest candle
EMA9 2/10 = 0.200 20.0%
EMA20 2/21 ≈ 0.095 9.5%

Example: Previous EMA9 = $100.00. The new 5m candle closes at $101.00.

  • EMA9 = 0.2 × 101.00 + 0.8 × 100.00 = $100.20
  • EMA20 (previous $100.00) = 0.0952 × 101.00 + 0.9048 × 100.00 = $100.10

EMA9 moved twice as far as EMA20 in response to the same candle. That is why EMA9 “leads”.

4.2.1 How much time does EMA9 or EMA20 “cover” on a 5-minute chart?

  • EMA9 ≈ 9 × 5 min = ~45 minutes of bars.
  • EMA20 ≈ 20 × 5 min = ~100 minutes.

This is only an intuitive description. An EMA never fully forgets old data: every past candle keeps a shrinking weight. A useful fact: for any EMA(N), roughly 86–87% of the total weight lies in the most recent N candles, since 1 − (1 − α)^N ≈ 1 − e⁻² ≈ 0.865. So “EMA9 ≈ the last 45 minutes” is a good mental model, as long as you remember the older bars still count a little.

4.3 EMA alignment vs EMA crossover

Concept Meaning v1 usage
Alignment (state) EMA9 is currently above (or below) EMA20. v1 uses alignment in the scanner and alert.
Crossover (event) EMA9 crosses EMA20 on this candle. v1 uses the crossover only as Exit C (trend failure).
Slope Is the EMA rising or falling? Discretionary check. Prefer both EMAs sloping in the trade direction.
Separation Gap between EMA9 and EMA20. Ranking. Clear separation = established trend. Very wide = possibly overextended.
Compression EMAs nearly touching and flat. Chop. Signals are less reliable.

EMA9 > EMA20 → the short-term average is above the medium-term average, so recent prices are higher (bullish bias). EMA9 < EMA20 → bearish bias.

Separation example: EMA9 $100.40, EMA20 $100.10. Separation = $0.30 = 0.30 ÷ 100.10 ≈ 0.30% of price. Compare across candidates in percentage terms, not dollars.

4.4 SMA vs EMA

SMA EMA
Weighting Equal Recent-heavy
Speed Slower Faster
False signals Fewer, but later More, but earlier
v1 Not used Used (9, 20)

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating every EMA crossover as a trade. In sideways markets EMAs cross back and forth constantly (“whipsaw”). v1 requires several confirming conditions for exactly this reason.

5 RSI — Relative Strength Index

5.1 Plain English

RSI measures how strongly price has been rising versus falling over recent candles, on a 0–100 scale. High RSI = recent gains dominated. Low RSI = recent losses dominated.

5.2 Technical definition [IND] (Wilder’s RSI)

  1. For each candle: Gain = max(Close − PrevClose, 0); Loss = max(PrevClose − Close, 0).
  2. AvgGain and AvgLoss = Wilder-smoothed averages over N candles (N = 14 for RSI14).
  3. RS = AvgGain ÷ AvgLoss.
  4. RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + RS).

“14” means the averages cover 14 candles. On a 5m chart that is 70 minutes of bars, with Wilder smoothing keeping some memory of older bars.

AvgGain AvgLoss RS RSI
0.30 0.15 2.00 100 − 100/3 = 66.7
0.20 0.20 1.00 50.0
0.10 0.20 0.50 100 − 100/1.5 = 33.3
— — 1.22 55 (your LONG threshold)
— — 0.82 45 (your SHORT threshold)

5.3 70/30, “overbought” and “oversold” — and why RSI > 70 is NOT a sell signal

Reading Textbook label What it really means
> 70 “Overbought” Strong upward momentum. In trends, RSI can stay above 70 for hours.
< 30 “Oversold” Strong downward momentum. It can stay there.
50 Neutral Gains and losses balanced.

There are two interpretations:

  • Momentum interpretation (v1 uses this): RSI above 55 = upside momentum confirmed; below 45 = downside momentum.
  • Reversal interpretation: extreme RSI (> 80 / < 20) = move may be exhausted and a snap-back is likely. v1 uses this only as a caution in ranking.

WHY RSI 75 IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A SHORT

RSI 75 says buyers have dominated recently. Shorting it is betting that the strongest buyers of the day are about to quit, with no evidence other than “it went up a lot”. In v1, a SHORT requires price below VWAP, EMA9 < EMA20 and RSI < 45. An RSI-75 stock fails every one of those.

5.4 Divergence

Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high, so momentum is fading. Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low, RSI a higher low. Divergences are warnings, not triggers, and are not part of v1.

5.5 How v1 uses RSI

MY v1 RULE — RSI14 (5m)

Hard filter (scanner/alert) Preferred zone (ranking) Caution zone
LONG RSI > 55 55–70 > 75–80: exhaustion risk
SHORT RSI < 45 30–45 < 20–25: exhaustion / snap-back risk

When NOT to rely on RSI: in the first ~15 minutes of the session (very few bars since the open, and the overnight gap distorts it), in illiquid names, and as a stand-alone signal.

6 Volume and Relative Volume (RVOL)

6.1 Raw volume vs average volume

Term Meaning Example
Volume (per candle) Shares traded during that candle. The 10:00–10:05 candle traded 250,000 shares.
Average volume Mean of volume over N candles. 20-day average daily volume = 4.2M shares.
Volume MA20 (Daily) The 20-period simple moving average of daily volume. v1 filter: > 1,000,000 shares [RULE].

Why 1M+ daily volume? Liquidity. A stock trading 1M+ shares a day typically has tight spreads and enough depth that a few-hundred-share order barely moves it. For the S&P 500 this filter removes very few names, but it guards the system if you later expand the universe.

6.2 Relative Volume (RVOL)

Plain English: “Is this candle busier than normal?” RVOL compares current volume with its own recent average.

Technical (TrendSpider’s Relative Volume indicator) [TS]: RVOL = Volume ÷ MA(Volume, Length). The inputs are:

Parameter Your value Meaning [TS]
Length 20 Number of periods in the volume average.
MA Type SMA Averaging method. Options include SMA, EMA and HullMA.
Base 1 The benchmark/reference line. Base 1 = “average volume”. The help example: a base of 1.1 marks volume 10% above average.
RVOL Meaning
0.5 Half the usual volume: quiet, low conviction.
1.0 Normal.
1.5 50% above normal. v1 alert threshold.
2.0 Double normal: strong participation. v1 scanner threshold.
3.0+ Unusual activity: news, a breakout, or opening/closing distortion.

Example: the 5m candle traded 300,000 shares; the 20-candle average is 100,000 → RVOL = 3.0.

6.3 Why high RVOL matters, and why extreme RVOL can be dangerous

  • High RVOL = many participants agree on the move. Breakouts on high volume fail less often than breakouts on low volume [IND].
  • Extreme RVOL (e.g., 8–15+) often means news, a halt-resume, an index rebalance, or a climax. Spreads widen and candles get enormous, so stop distances explode. The “trend” may be a single-candle spike that reverses.

VERIFY — opening and closing distortion in a bar-based RVOL

TrendSpider documents RVOL as volume relative to its moving average. It does not document a “time-of-day” adjustment. If RVOL is bar-to-recent-bars (likely), then:

  • At 9:30–9:45, the first 5m bars are compared with the previous 20 bars. Those are mostly yesterday afternoon, or thin pre-market bars if Extended Hours is on. Opening bars are naturally 3–10× busier, so RVOL is inflated at the open for almost every stock.
  • At 15:50–16:00, closing-auction flows inflate volume again. RVOL of 12 at the close is normal and meaningless for v1.
  • After hours, a single block print against thin bars can create RVOL in the tens.

This is one reason v1 says observe only from 9:30–9:40. Check on your chart by comparing the RVOL readings of the 9:30 bar on several quiet stocks.

6.4 Volume vs RVOL

Volume RVOL
Units Shares Ratio (no units)
Comparable across stocks? No (AAPL trades far more than most) Yes: 2.0 means “twice its own normal” for any stock
v1 use Daily MA20 > 1M (liquidity) 5m RVOL > 2.0 (scanner), > 1.5 (alert)

7 ATR — Average True Range

7.1 Plain English

ATR measures how much a stock typically moves per candle, ignoring direction. It measures volatility, not trend.

7.2 Technical definition [IND]

  • True Range (TR) = the largest of:
    1. High − Low
    2. |High − Previous Close|
    3. |Low − Previous Close|
  • ATR(14) = Wilder-smoothed average of TR over 14 candles.

The second and third terms capture gaps: if a candle opens far from the prior close, that move counts.

TR example: Previous close $50.00. Candle H $50.80, L $50.10.

  • H − L = 0.70; |H − PC| = 0.80; |L − PC| = 0.10 → TR = $0.80. The gap up counts.

7.3 Why a fixed $0.50 stop does not make sense for every stock

Stock 5m ATR A $0.50 stop equals Interpretation
A ($40 stock) $0.08 6.3 ATR Absurdly wide. You give back far too much.
B ($150 stock) $0.45 1.1 ATR Reasonable.
C ($480 stock) $1.60 0.3 ATR Noise will stop you out almost immediately.

Volatility-adjusted stops keep the “meaning” of a stop consistent across stocks.

7.4 ATR multiples, position sizing and “do not chase”

  • ATR stop: Stop = Entry − k × ATR (LONG) or Entry + k × ATR (SHORT). k is typically 1–2 on intraday charts [IND].
  • ATR and size: because risk/share rises with ATR, shares fall automatically when you size by risk (Chapter 18). Volatile stocks get smaller positions.
  • ATR and chasing: if price is already more than ~1 ATR beyond your planned entry, you have missed it. If the signal candle’s range is more than ~2× ATR, the candle is “abnormally large” (Chapter 21).

MY v1 RULE — ATR is reference only

v1 stops are the signal-candle low/high, not ATR. ATR is used only as a sanity check for “candle too large”, “stop too wide” and “too extended”. An ATR-based stop is a candidate for v2 (Chapter 22).

8 Secondary Indicators — Quick Reference (NOT part of v1)

Indicator Plain English Formula sketch Typical use Caution
MACD (12,26,9) Momentum from the gap between two EMAs. MACD = EMA12 − EMA26; Signal = EMA9(MACD); Histogram = MACD − Signal. Momentum shifts, crossovers. Lagging; overlaps heavily with EMA9/20.
Bollinger Bands (20,2) Volatility envelope. Middle = SMA20; Bands = SMA20 ± 2 × std. dev. Squeeze → expansion; extension measure. Touching a band is not a signal by itself.
ADX (14) Trend strength (not direction). Derived from +DI/−DI smoothing; 0–100. ADX > 25 = trending; < 20 = chop. Lagging; direction comes from +DI/−DI.
Stochastic (14,3,3) Where the close sits in the recent range. %K = (C − LowestLow) ÷ (HighestHigh − LowestLow) × 100. Overbought/oversold in ranges. Pins at extremes in trends.
Relative Strength (RS) Stock performance vs a benchmark (e.g., SPY). RS = Price_stock ÷ Price_SPY (or % change difference). Leaders vs laggards. Not the same as RSI.
ADR (Average Daily Range) Typical daily high-to-low range. Mean of (High − Low) over N days, often as % of price. How much room is left today. Ignores gaps (ATR includes them).
Support/Resistance Zones where price reversed before. Swing highs/lows, prior day H/L, round numbers. Targets, obstacles. Zones, not lines.
Pivot points (classic) Formula levels from the prior day. P = (H + L + C) ÷ 3; R1 = 2P − L; S1 = 2P − H. Intraday reference levels. Self-fulfilling at best.

RSI vs Relative Strength: RSI compares a stock with its own past. Relative Strength compares a stock with another instrument. A stock can have RSI 65 and still be weaker than SPY.

9 Multi-Timeframe Analysis

9.1 Why a 1-minute chart is noisy for a beginner

On a 1m chart, a single large order, a spread flicker or a news headline produces a “signal”. Indicators flip constantly, and you face many more decisions per hour, each with less information. The 5m chart filters much of that noise while still giving intraday timing.

9.2 Why v1 uses 5m for entries and 15m for confirmation

Timeframe Role Question it answers
Daily Universe/context Is the stock liquid, in my price band, and moving ≥ 1% today in my direction?
15-minute Confirmation (higher timeframe) Is the bigger intraday trend on my side? (15m Close > EMA20 for LONG.)
5-minute Entry/timing Is there a setup right now, and where exactly is my entry and stop?

“Higher-timeframe confirmation” means requiring the larger timeframe to agree with your trade direction before acting on a smaller-timeframe signal. One 15m candle contains three 5m candles (e.g., 9:30, 9:35 and 9:40 make up the 9:30 15m candle). An EMA20 on 15m spans ~300 minutes, roughly the whole morning. It is approximately comparable to (but not identical to) an EMA60 on the 5m chart.

9.3 Alignment and conflict

15m 5m Interpretation v1 action
Up (Close > EMA20) Up setup Aligned. You trade with the tide. LONG allowed
Down Down setup Aligned. SHORT allowed
Down Up setup Conflict. The 5m bounce is likely a pullback inside a 15m downtrend, and sellers wait above. No LONG (fails the alert)
Up Down setup Conflict. Likely a dip in an uptrend. No SHORT

WHY “5m BULLISH BUT 15m BEARISH” IS DANGEROUS

A 5m rally inside a 15m downtrend often runs straight into the 15m EMA20 or VWAP from below, exactly where higher-timeframe sellers re-enter. Your 2R target sits above a ceiling, while your stop sits in a falling trend.

VERIFY — how a 15m condition is evaluated inside a 5m alert

TrendSpider checks a Multi-Factor Alert when the smallest-timeframe candle closes (here: every 5 minutes) [TS]. Its documentation notes that a larger-timeframe condition uses the last calculated data point, and can become untrue when that larger candle closes, which can make an alert look like it “misfired” [TS]. In practice, at 10:05 the 15m condition may be reading the still-forming 10:00–10:15 candle. Always re-check the 15m chart yourself when the alert fires.

PART IV — MY DAY TRADING SYSTEM v1 (LEVEL 4)

10 System Overview and Universe

10.1 The v1 system on one page

Stage LONG SHORT Tool
Universe S&P 500, $10–$500, Daily Volume MA20 > 1M same Scanner
Candidate scan Bullish momentum scanner Bearish momentum scanner TrendSpider Market Scanner
Rank RVOL, VWAP distance, EMA separation, RSI 55–70, daily move, 15m, extension mirror (RSI 30–45) Your judgement / Sidekick
Candidate list Static LONG list Static SHORT list Watchlists
Setup alert RB v1 – LONG Setup (6 AND conditions) RB v1 – SHORT Setup Multi-Factor Alerts
Inspect Full checklist + Do-Not-Take list same You
Entry Break of signal-candle high + small buffer Break of signal-candle low − buffer Trading widget
Stop Signal-candle low Signal-candle high Trading widget

Exits A stop · B 2R · C trend failure · D time stop same You + broker

10.2 Universe

MY v1 RULE — Universe

  • Primary universe: S&P 500 constituents.
  • Price: $10–$500 (on the 5-minute close).
  • Liquidity: Daily Volume 20-period MA > 1,000,000 shares.
  • Session: Regular session (09:30–16:00 ET) initially. Extended hours are not traded.
Filter What it removes Why
S&P 500 Small caps, illiquid names, most “meme” stocks Liquidity, tight spreads, easier to borrow for shorts, fewer halts.
≥ $10 Low-priced stocks On low-priced stocks a one-cent tick is a large percentage of price, and spreads are relatively wider. (Few S&P 500 names are below $10.)
≤ $500 Very high-priced stocks At 0.25% risk ($250), a $900 stock with a $4 stop yields only 62 shares. That works mathematically, but sizing becomes coarse and 2R targets are large in dollars.
Volume MA20 > 1M Thinly traded names Fills close to plan, low slippage.
Regular session Pre/post-market Thin liquidity, wide spreads, limit-only order rules, unreliable indicators.

11 The Bullish Candidate Scanner

Scanner name: RB v1 – Regular-Session Bullish Momentum Search in: S&P 500 · Logic: ALL of the following · Current Candle: ON · Ext. Hours: OFF

# Condition (as built) Timeframe What it contributes Overlaps with
1 Close > 10 (constant) 5m Price floor —
2 Close < 500 (constant) 5m Price ceiling —
3 Volume MA(20) > 1,000,000 Daily Liquidity —
4 Relative Volume (20) > 2.0 5m The stock is in play right now: twice its normal activity Partly with #5 (moves often need volume)
5 Close is above Close 1 candle ago by at least 1% Daily The stock is up ≥ 1% on the day, so it has daily-level directional bias #6, #8 (up days tend to be above VWAP and higher RSI)
6 Close > VWAP 5m Intraday buyers in control #7, #8
7 EMA(9) > EMA(20) 5m Short-term trend up #6, #8
8 RSI(14) > 55 5m Upside momentum #6, #7
9 Close > EMA(20) 15m Higher-timeframe trend up #7

11.0.1 Understanding the overlap

Conditions 6, 7 and 8 are highly correlated. In a steady uptrend, all three are usually true together. That is fine: overlapping conditions make the scan stricter about the same idea (an intraday uptrend) rather than adding new information. The genuinely independent information comes from:

  • #3 Liquidity (can I trade it efficiently?)
  • #4 RVOL (is anyone actually participating?)
  • #5 Daily change (is there a daily directional story?)
  • #9 15m trend (does the bigger picture agree?)

WHY IT MATTERS — three timeframes is the scanner limit

This scan uses exactly three timeframes: 5m, 15m and Daily. TrendSpider’s scanner supports up to three timeframes at once [TS]. You cannot add, for example, a 1-hour condition without removing one of these.

VERIFY — the exact “by at least X%” wording

Your build uses a Daily condition of the form “Close … above … Close 1 candle ago … by at least 1%”. TrendSpider documents candle offsets in its scripting help, but the official pages reviewed did not show the exact “by at least” control. Document the precise wording you see in the editor in Appendix C (SS-14) so it can be rebuilt identically.

With Current Candle ON, condition #5 compares today’s developing daily candle (i.e., the current price) to yesterday’s close. That is exactly “current price is ≥ 1% above previous close”.

12 The Bearish Candidate Scanner

Scanner name: RB v1 – Regular-Session Bearish Momentum Search in: S&P 500 · Logic: ALL · Current Candle: ON · Ext. Hours: OFF

# Condition TF Contribution LONG counterpart
1 Close > 10 5m Price floor (not inverted: still a price band) same
2 Close < 500 5m Price ceiling (not inverted) same
3 Volume MA(20) > 1,000,000 D Liquidity (not inverted) same
4 Relative Volume (20) > 2.0 5m In play (not inverted: high volume matters both ways) same
5 Close is below Close 1 candle ago by at least 1% D Down ≥ 1% on the day inverted
6 Close < VWAP 5m Sellers in control intraday inverted
7 EMA(9) < EMA(20) 5m Short-term trend down inverted
8 RSI(14) < 45 5m Downside momentum inverted (55 → 45, symmetric around 50)
9 Close < EMA(20) 15m Higher-timeframe trend down inverted

COMMON MISTAKE — inverting everything

Only directional conditions are mirrored. Price band, liquidity and RVOL stay the same for shorts. An “RVOL < 2” bearish scan would find quiet stocks, which is the opposite of what you want.

13 The LONG Alert — “RB v1 – LONG Setup”

MY v1 RULE — LONG alert (ALL conditions, AND logic)

  1. 5m Close > VWAP
  2. 5m EMA9 > EMA20
  3. 5m RSI14 > 55
  4. 5m RVOL20 > 1.5
  5. 5m Close > Open (the signal candle is green)
  6. 15m Close > EMA20
# Condition Plain English
1 Close > VWAP The signal candle closed above the day’s average cost.
2 EMA9 > EMA20 Short-term trend is up.
3 RSI14 > 55 Momentum is to the upside.
4 RVOL20 > 1.5 This candle traded at least 1.5× recent average volume.
5 Close > Open Buyers won this specific 5-minute period.
6 15m Close > EMA20 The bigger picture agrees.

13.1 AND vs OR logic

Logic TrendSpider label [TS] Fires when Example with 6 conditions
AND “All of the following” Every condition is true All 6 true → fires; 5 of 6 → no alert
OR “Any of the following” At least one is true Any single condition true → fires (far too often)
NOT “None of the following” None are true Used to exclude

v1 uses AND (“All of the following”) exclusively.

13.2 Why the alert uses RVOL > 1.5 while the scanner uses RVOL > 2.0

  1. Different jobs. The scanner asks “which stocks are in play today?”. A high bar (2.0) keeps the list short. The alert asks “is this particular candle supported by volume?”. Once a stock is already in play, a healthy continuation candle does not need double volume, and a pullback-resumption candle often has less volume than the initial surge.
  2. Avoiding missed setups. Requiring 2.0 on the trigger candle would miss many valid continuation entries.
  3. Partial vs complete candle. With Current Candle ON, the scanner’s RVOL may be computed on a partial candle, which understates volume early in the bar. The alert evaluates a completed 5m candle [TS: alerts are checked when the smallest-timeframe candle closes].

13.3 What the alert means — and what it does not mean

ALERT ≠ TRADE

The alert means: “Inspect this stock now.” It does not mean “buy”. After it fires you still must: verify the timestamp, identify the signal candle, run the Do-Not-Take checklist, compute entry/stop/size/target, and wait for the price to break the signal-candle high.

14 The SHORT Alert — “RB v1 – SHORT Setup”

MY v1 RULE — SHORT alert (ALL conditions)

  1. 5m Close < VWAP
  2. 5m EMA9 < EMA20
  3. 5m RSI14 < 45
  4. 5m RVOL20 > 1.5 (not inverted)
  5. 5m Close < Open (the signal candle is red)
  6. 15m Close < EMA20
# Plain English
1 The signal candle closed below the day’s average cost: sellers in control.
2 Short-term trend is down.
3 Momentum is to the downside.
4 Volume confirms participation (high volume matters in both directions).
5 Sellers won this 5-minute period.
6 The higher timeframe trend is down.

15 Candidate Ranking

15.1 Why the scanner returns too many stocks

On a strong trend day (e.g., the S&P 500 up 1.5%), dozens of stocks can pass the bullish scan at once, because the market lifts everything. You cannot watch 40 charts, and alerts are capped by plan (Chapter 28). Ranking narrows the list to the best 5–15.

15.2 Ranking factors

Factor How to measure LONG preferred SHORT preferred Red flag (either side)
RVOL 5m RVOL20 2–6 2–6 > 10 (news spike, climax)
Distance from VWAP (Close − VWAP) ÷ 5m ATR +0.2 to +1.5 ATR −0.2 to −1.5 ATR > 2.5 ATR away
EMA separation (EMA9 − EMA20) ÷ Price clearly positive (≈ 0.1–0.6%) clearly negative ≈ 0 (chop) or very wide (stretched)
RSI14 (5m) Indicator value 55–70 30–45 > 78 / < 22
Daily % move (Price − Prev close) ÷ Prev close +1% to +4% −1% to −4% > ±7–8% (exhaustion or news)
15m relationship Close vs 15m EMA20 and its slope above, EMA rising below, EMA falling flat 15m EMA
Overextension Count of consecutive same-colour 5m candles; distance from EMA20 ≤ 4–5 in a row ≤ 4–5 in a row parabolic, vertical moves

RECOMMENDATION — a simple 0–2 scoring rubric (not part of v1 until adopted)

Score each of the seven factors: 2 = preferred zone, 1 = acceptable, 0 = red flag. Maximum 14. Keep the top 10 for each direction, and discard anything with any 0 on VWAP distance, RSI or RVOL. Record the score in the journal (“Scanner ranking” column) so that after 50 trades you can test whether higher scores really perform better.

15.3 Why more momentum is not always better

Concept Plain English Why it hurts
FOMO (fear of missing out) Buying because it’s running and you feel left behind You buy late, near the top, with a wide stop.
Chasing Entering far beyond the planned trigger Risk/share is larger than planned, or the stop is no longer logical.
Overextension Price far from its averages (VWAP, EMA20) Little room for 2R before a snap-back.
Mean reversion Stretched prices tend to drift back toward an average The “rubber band” snaps back to VWAP.
Snap-back risk A sharp counter-move after an extended run Hits your stop before your target.

Numerical example. Stock A: price $101.20, VWAP $100.50, 5m ATR $0.40 → 1.75 ATR above VWAP. Stock B: price $103.60, VWAP $100.50, ATR $0.40 → 7.75 ATR above VWAP. B looks stronger, but a pull back merely halfway to VWAP is −$1.55, many times a typical stop. A is the better candidate.

16 Entry Rules

16.1 LONG entry

MY v1 RULE — LONG entry

  1. Alert fires. Identify the signal candle: the completed 5-minute candle that satisfied the alert.
  2. Do not automatically buy.
  3. Potential entry: break above the signal-candle high + a small buffer.
  4. Timing: if the break does not happen within roughly the next 1–2 five-minute candles, skip. Do not chase.

This timing rule is your trading rule, not a TrendSpider limitation.

What “break above the high + buffer” means. The signal candle’s high is the highest price buyers reached during that candle. A trade above that high shows buyers are still pushing beyond the signal: that is your confirmation. The buffer (a few cents) avoids entering on a single print that merely touches the high.

Example: Signal-candle High = $100.20 → entry trigger around $100.21–$100.25.

Stock price Suggested buffer [REC]
$10–$50 $0.01–$0.02
$50–$200 $0.02–$0.05
$200–$500 $0.05–$0.10

16.2 SHORT entry

MY v1 RULE — SHORT entry

Potential entry: break below the signal-candle low − small buffer, within roughly the next 1–2 five-minute candles. Otherwise skip.

Example: Signal-candle Low = $87.40 → entry around $87.35–$87.39.

16.3 Why require confirmation?

The alert fires on a candle that already closed. Many signal candles are the end of a burst, not the start. Requiring the next candle(s) to trade beyond the signal extreme filters out setups where momentum immediately stalls. The cost is a slightly worse entry price. The benefit is avoiding many failed setups. Whether that trade-off is profitable for your system is a question for your journal (Chapter 39).

16.4 Situations and what to do

Situation v1 action Reason
Price already ran too far (beyond trigger by > ~0.5R) Skip Your risk/share is now bigger than planned and the 2R target is further away.
Signal is ~10 minutes old (two candles have passed) Skip unless the trigger has not yet been hit and price is still near it The 1–2 candle rule.
Price never breaks the candle Cancel any pending order after 1–2 candles; no trade No confirmation.
Candle is enormous (range > ~2× 5m ATR) Skip, or treat as a v2 discretionary case The stop at the other end is too wide, and the candle may be exhaustion.
Spread is wide (> ~10% of risk/share) Skip Spread eats your edge.
Stock gaps violently (e.g., a 1-minute spike through trigger on news) Skip Fill quality is unknown, and news-driven moves don’t respect technicals.
Major resistance just above (LONG) / support just below (SHORT) within 2R Skip or require reward ≥ 2R before the level No room to reach target.

17 Stop-Loss

17.1 Stop-loss methods compared

Method LONG stop SHORT stop Pros Cons
Signal-candle extreme (v1) Signal-candle low Signal-candle high Objective, structural: if price takes out the whole signal candle, the setup failed Width depends on candle size; large candles = wide stops
VWAP Below VWAP Above VWAP Ties to the thesis “price above VWAP” May be far away; VWAP moves
ATR Entry − k × ATR Entry + k × ATR Volatility-consistent Not tied to structure
Support/Resistance Below support Above resistance Uses market structure Subjective; obvious levels get “run”
Percentage Entry × (1 − p%) Entry × (1 + p%) Simple Ignores volatility and structure

17.2 Why v1 uses the signal-candle low/high

MY v1 RULE — Stop

  • LONG stop = signal-candle low.
  • SHORT stop = signal-candle high.
  • If the logical stop creates unacceptable risk, skip the trade. Never move the stop artificially closer to make the trade “fit”.

Logic: the signal candle is the evidence for your trade. If price trades back through the entire signal candle, the buying (or selling) pressure that created it has been fully reversed, and the setup is invalid.

When this stop may be too wide:

  • The signal candle is very large (> ~2× ATR).
  • The stock is high-priced and volatile.
  • The resulting position, after the notional cap, is so small that the trade is not meaningful.

When it may be too tight:

  • The signal candle is tiny (e.g., $0.08 range), so the spread and normal noise can stop you out. Watch the Do-Not-Take list.

COMMON MISTAKE — squeezing the stop

“The real stop is $1.20 away, so I’ll use $0.50 to get a bigger position.” This replaces a logical stop with an arbitrary one. Price will often hit the arbitrary stop and then go to your target. If the logical stop is too far, the correct answer is a smaller position or no trade.

18 Risk Management and Position Sizing

This is the most important chapter in the manual. You cannot control whether a trade wins. You can always control how much it loses.

18.1 Inputs vs outputs

MY v1 RULE — Risk per trade

Maximum intended loss per trade = 0.25% of current portfolio equity. At $100,000 → $250.

The key mental shift:

Beginner thinking Professional thinking
Input (you choose) “I’ll buy 500 shares.” “I will lose at most $250 if wrong.”
Output (calculated) “My loss will be… whatever happens.” “Therefore I can buy N shares.”

Share quantity is an OUTPUT. Maximum loss is an INPUT.

18.2 The formulas

Quantity LONG SHORT
Dollar risk (R in $) Equity × 0.25% Equity × 0.25%
Risk per share Entry − Stop Stop − Entry
Position size (shares) floor(Dollar risk ÷ Risk per share) same
Actual dollar risk Shares × Risk per share same
2R target Entry + 2 × Risk per share Entry − 2 × Risk per share
Notional (position value) Shares × Entry Shares × Entry

“floor” means round down to a whole share. Rounding up would risk slightly more than your limit.

18.3 The notional cap (recommendation)

Risk-based sizing alone can create huge positions when the stop is tight. Example: a $200 stock with a $0.20 stop → 1,250 shares = $250,000 notional, 2.5× your equity. A single halt or news gap through your stop could cost many multiples of $250.

RECOMMENDATION — Position notional cap for v1 paper trading

  • Maximum notional per position = 50% of equity ($50,000 at $100,000).
  • Maximum total notional across all open positions = 100% of equity (no reliance on margin leverage).
  • Shares = the smaller of floor(Dollar risk ÷ Risk/share) and floor(Notional cap ÷ Entry).
  • When the cap binds, your actual risk is below $250. That is acceptable: the $250 is a maximum, not a target.

Status: recommendation. Adopt it explicitly (and log it in the Change Log) or reject it.

18.4 Ten-plus worked examples

All examples use 0.25% risk and the 50%-of-equity notional cap. Read each one slowly.

18.4.1 Example 1 — LONG, high-priced stock, cap binds

  • Equity $100,000 → dollar risk $250; notional cap $50,000.
  • Signal candle: High $230.40, Low $229.90. Buffer $0.02.
  • Entry = $230.42; Stop = $229.90.
  • Risk/share = 230.42 − 229.90 = $0.52.
  • Risk-based shares = floor(250 ÷ 0.52) = floor(480.77) = 480.
  • Notional check: 480 × 230.42 = $110,601.60 → exceeds $50,000.
  • Cap shares = floor(50,000 ÷ 230.42) = floor(216.99) = 216 (216 × 230.42 = $49,770.72).
  • Final: 216 shares. Actual risk = 216 × 0.52 = $112.32.
  • 2R target = 230.42 + 2 × 0.52 = $231.46. Potential reward = 216 × 1.04 = $224.64.

18.4.2 Example 2 — LONG, mid-priced stock, normal case

  • Signal: High $45.80, Low $45.35. Entry $45.82; Stop $45.35.
  • Risk/share = $0.47.
  • Shares = floor(250 ÷ 0.47) = floor(531.9) = 531. Actual risk = 531 × 0.47 = $249.57.
  • Notional = 531 × 45.82 = $24,330.42 (under the cap ✓).
  • 2R target = 45.82 + 0.94 = $46.76.

18.4.3 Example 3 — SHORT, normal case

  • Signal: High $88.85, Low $88.10. Entry (break of low − $0.02) = $88.08; Stop = $88.85.
  • Risk/share = Stop − Entry = 88.85 − 88.08 = $0.77.
  • Shares = floor(250 ÷ 0.77) = floor(324.7) = 324. Actual risk = $249.48.
  • Notional = 324 × 88.08 = $28,537.92 ✓.
  • 2R target = 88.08 − 2 × 0.77 = $86.54.

18.4.4 Example 4 — LONG, enormous signal candle (math works, checklist says skip)

  • $300 stock. Signal: High $302.50, Low $299.00. Entry $302.53; Stop $299.00.
  • Risk/share = $3.53. Shares = floor(250 ÷ 3.53) = floor(70.8) = 70. Risk $247.10. Notional $21,177.10.
  • 2R target = 302.53 + 7.06 = $309.59.
  • But: 5m ATR ≈ $1.20, so the candle range of $3.50 ≈ 2.9 ATR: an abnormally large candle. Reaching +$7.06 needs ~6 more ATRs of movement. Skip (Do-Not-Take list).

18.4.5 Example 5 — SHORT, low-priced stock

  • Signal: High $24.85, Low $24.60. Entry $24.59; Stop $24.85.
  • Risk/share = $0.26. Shares = floor(250 ÷ 0.26) = floor(961.5) = 961. Risk $249.86.
  • Notional = 961 × 24.59 = $23,630.99 ✓.
  • 2R target = 24.59 − 0.52 = $24.07.

18.4.6 Example 6 — LONG, tiny stop, cap binds hard

  • $120 stock. Signal: High $120.08, Low $119.98. Entry $120.10; Stop $119.98.
  • Risk/share = $0.12. Risk-based shares = floor(250 ÷ 0.12) = 2,083 → notional $250,168 ✗.
  • Cap shares = floor(50,000 ÷ 120.10) = 416. Actual risk = 416 × 0.12 = $49.92.
  • Also check: if the spread is $0.02, it equals 17% of risk/share. A tiny stop is very vulnerable to noise. Consider skipping.

18.4.7 Example 7 — Equity has fallen (risk shrinks automatically)

  • Equity now $98,600 → dollar risk = 0.25% × 98,600 = $246.50.
  • LONG: Entry $60.25; Stop $59.80 → risk/share $0.45.
  • Shares = floor(246.50 ÷ 0.45) = floor(547.8) = 547. Risk $246.15. Notional $32,956.75 ✓.
  • 2R target = $61.15.

18.4.8 Example 8 — Equity has grown, cap uses current equity

  • Equity $103,200 → dollar risk $258; notional cap 50% = $51,600.
  • SHORT: Entry $152.40; Stop $153.10 → risk/share $0.70.
  • Risk shares = floor(258 ÷ 0.70) = floor(368.6) = 368 → notional 368 × 152.40 = $56,083.20 ✗.
  • Cap shares = floor(51,600 ÷ 152.40) = floor(338.6) = 338. Actual risk = 338 × 0.70 = $236.60.
  • 2R target = 152.40 − 1.40 = $151.00.

18.4.9 Example 9 — The effect of slippage

  • Take Example 2 (531 shares, planned risk $249.57).
  • Entry actually fills at $45.87 (+$0.05 slippage); stop actually fills at $45.31 (−$0.04).
  • Actual loss/share = 45.87 − 45.31 = $0.56 → loss = 531 × 0.56 = $297.36 ≈ −1.19R.
  • Lesson: stops are not guaranteed prices. A −1R plan often becomes −1.1R to −1.3R in fast markets.
  • Optional (REC): size on (risk/share + expected slippage). With $0.03 expected slippage: floor(250 ÷ 0.50) = 500 shares.

18.4.10 Example 10 — Large price, unrealistic target

  • $480 stock. Signal: High $484.00, Low $478.50. Entry $484.03; Stop $478.50.
  • Risk/share = $5.53 → shares = floor(250 ÷ 5.53) = 45. Risk $248.85. Notional $21,781.35 ✓.
  • 2R target = 484.03 + 11.06 = $495.09.
  • If this stock’s entire typical day (ADR) is about $9, a further $11 move after an already large candle is unlikely. Realistic reward < 2R → skip.

18.4.11 Example 11 — Two positions at once

  • Open: LONG A risking $249.57 (Example 2) and SHORT B risking $249.48 (Example 3).
  • Total open risk = $499.05 = 0.50% of equity.
  • A third trade risking $250 would bring open risk to ~0.75%.

18.5 Portfolio-level risk concepts

Concept Meaning Example
Trade risk Max loss on one trade $250
Open (portfolio) risk Sum of all open trade risks 3 trades × $250 = $750 = 0.75%
Simultaneous-position risk Several stops can be hit together in a market-wide move SPY drops 0.5% in 5 minutes → every LONG stops out
Concentration Too much exposure in one name or sector 3 semiconductor LONGs = effectively one big bet
Correlated positions Positions that move together NVDA, AMD and AVGO LONGs typically move together
Gap risk Price jumps past your stop (halt, news) Stop at $99.50, next print $98.20
Slippage Worse fills than planned Example 9
Fees Commissions, regulatory fees, borrow fees Alpaca paper does not simulate regulatory or borrow fees [ALP]. Real trading has small SEC/FINRA fees on sales.

RECOMMENDATION — Conservative paper-trading portfolio limits

Limit Value Why
Max open risk 1.0% of equity ($1,000) Equivalent to 4 full-risk trades
Max concurrent positions (first 20 trades) 2 Lets you learn the workflow without overload
Max concurrent positions (after 20 trades) 3–4
Max positions in the same sector and direction 2 Correlation
Daily loss limit −1.0% realised ($1,000) or 3 consecutive losses → stop trading for the day Prevents tilt / revenge trading
Weekly loss limit −2.5% → stop, review journal before next session Forces review
Max notional 50% per position, 100% total Leverage and gap protection

Status: recommendations. Not part of v1 until you adopt them.

19 R-Multiples and Expectancy

19.1 What “R” means

Plain English: R is your risk on the trade. Expressing results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes.

Term Meaning Example (entry $100, stop $99.50, risk $0.50)
1R A gain equal to your initial risk Price at $100.50
2R A gain of twice your risk (v1 target) Price at $101.00
−1R A full planned loss Stopped at $99.50
+0.5R Half your risk in profit Price at $100.25
R result (Exit − Entry) ÷ Risk/share for LONG; (Entry − Exit) ÷ Risk/share for SHORT Exit $100.80 → +0.8 ÷ 0.5 = +1.6R

For a SHORT at $100 with stop $100.50: 1R = $99.50, 2R = $99.00, −1R = $100.50.

MY v1 RULE — Profit target

Initial profit target = 2R.

19.2 Expectancy — how a sub-50% win rate can be profitable

Expectancy (in R) = (Win rate × Average win in R) − (Loss rate × Average loss in R)

Scenario Win rate Avg win Avg loss Expectancy per trade Over 100 trades at $250/R
A: textbook 2R 40% 2.0R 1.0R 0.40×2 − 0.60×1 = +0.20R +20R = +$5,000
B: realistic (some early exits, slippage) 40% 1.6R 1.1R 0.64 − 0.66 = −0.02R −2R = −$500
C: lower win rate 30% 2.0R 1.0R 0.60 − 0.70 = −0.10R −$2,500
D: higher win rate, smaller wins 55% 1.0R 1.0R 0.55 − 0.45 = +0.10R +$2,500
E: good execution 45% 1.8R 1.0R 0.81 − 0.55 = +0.26R +$6,500

Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + Average win ÷ Average loss). For a clean 2R target: 1 ÷ 3 = 33.3%.

WHY IT MATTERS — Scenario B

The difference between A and B is small things: exiting a little early, slightly worse fills, a few −1.2R losses. Together they turn a winning system into a losing one. Execution discipline is part of the edge.

20 Exit Rules

MY v1 RULE — Exits (whichever comes first)

Exit LONG SHORT
A — Stop-loss Price trades at the signal-candle low (stop order fills) Price trades at the signal-candle high
B — 2R target Price reaches Entry + 2R (limit order fills) Price reaches Entry − 2R
C — Trend failure A 5m candle closes below VWAP, or EMA9 crosses below EMA20 A 5m candle closes above VWAP, or EMA9 crosses above EMA20
D — Time stop After ~6 five-minute candles (~30 min), if the trade has not reached ~+0.5R, consider exiting same

20.1 How each exit is executed

Exit Mechanism Who acts
A Resting stop order at the broker (the Stop Loss field) Automatic
B Resting limit order (the Take Profit field) Automatic
C Check at each 5m candle close; if triggered, close the position manually (market order or “X” in Open Positions) and make sure the remaining stop/target orders are cancelled You
D At ~30 minutes after entry, check progress You

VERIFY — orphaned orders after a manual exit

If you close a position manually, confirm that its Stop Loss and Take Profit orders are cancelled. Otherwise a leftover order could later open a new, unintended position. TrendSpider’s widget shows Pending Orders, and you can cancel with the X [TS]. Also check the Alpaca paper dashboard.

20.2 Clarifying the time-stop wording

Your rule says “has not reached approximately +0.5R”. This can be read two ways:

  1. Max favourable excursion (MFE): price has never traded at +0.5R during the 30 minutes.
  2. Current price: the trade is currently below +0.5R at the 30-minute mark.

v1 keeps your wording (“consider exiting”). Record both the MFE and the current R at minute 30 in your journal. After 50 trades you can test which reading (if either) improves results. The time stop must be validated through paper trading/backtesting rather than assumed optimal.

20.3 Exit priority example

LONG at $100.25, stop $99.75 (risk $0.50), target $101.25.

  • 10:15 entry. 10:30 price $100.60 (+0.7R). 10:40 a 5m candle closes at $100.30 below VWAP ($100.35) → Exit C at ≈ $100.30 = +0.1R.
  • Without Exit C the trade might have recovered, or might have stopped out at −1R. Exit C trades some winners for smaller losses. Your journal decides whether that helps.

20.4 Techniques intentionally NOT in v1

Technique What it is Why it is excluded from v1 initially
Trailing stop Stop follows price at a distance (e.g., 1 ATR below the high) Adds discretion and changes the R distribution. Test later. Alpaca trailing stops do not trigger outside regular hours [ALP].
Partial profit-taking Sell half at 1R, let the rest run Complicates sizing and journal analysis. TrendSpider’s Strategy Tester cannot backtest partial exits [TS].
Break-even stop Move stop to entry after +1R Feels safe, but often converts eventual winners into scratches. Must be proven with data.

Principle: change one thing at a time, and only after you have a baseline of 50–100 v1 trades.

21 The “Do Not Take the Trade” Checklist

Use it after the alert fires and before placing any order. Any single YES = skip. Thresholds marked [REC] are suggestions.

21.1 LONG version

# Question Skip if YES
1 Is the signal candle’s range > ~2× the 5m ATR? [REC] ☐
2 Is price more than ~2.5 ATR above VWAP? [REC] ☐
3 Did the stock gap up > ~7% today, or is it up > ~7–8%? [REC] ☐
4 Is RSI14 > ~78 (exhaustion)? [REC] ☐
5 Is major resistance (prior day high, round number, HOD) closer than the 2R target? ☐
6 Is the spread wide (> ~10% of risk/share), or is the stock illiquid right now? ☐
7 Is there breaking news / a halt / a news-driven spike? ☐
8 Is the stock reporting earnings today or tonight? ☐
9 Is the alert stale (> ~2 five-minute candles since signal close)? ☐
10 Has price already moved > ~0.5R past the trigger (missed entry)? ☐
11 Does the logical stop create unacceptable risk (position after cap too small, or stop distance > ~2 ATR)? ☐
12 Is realistic reward < 2R? ☐
13 Would this exceed open-risk / sector / correlation limits? ☐
14 Is the market regime strongly opposite (e.g., SPY below VWAP and falling hard)? ☐
15 Is it 09:30–09:40 or after ~15:30? [REC: last-30-minute caution] ☐
16 Have I hit my daily loss limit? ☐

21.2 SHORT version

# Question Skip if YES
1 Is the signal candle’s range > ~2× 5m ATR? ☐
2 Is price more than ~2.5 ATR below VWAP? ☐
3 Did the stock gap down > ~7%, or is it down > ~7–8%? (Also check SSR: down ≥ 10% from prior close [REG].) ☐
4 Is RSI14 < ~22 (exhaustion)? ☐
5 Is major support (prior day low, round number, LOD) closer than the 2R target? ☐
6 Wide spread / illiquid / not shortable (hard to borrow)? ☐
7 Breaking news / halt? ☐
8 Earnings today/tonight? ☐
9 Stale alert? ☐
10 Missed entry (> ~0.5R past trigger)? ☐
11 Stop risk unacceptable? ☐
12 Realistic reward < 2R? ☐
13 Exposure limits exceeded? ☐
14 Market regime strongly opposite (e.g., SPY ripping above VWAP)? ☐
15 09:30–09:40 or after ~15:30? ☐
16 Daily loss limit hit? ☐

22 Potential v2 Improvements

NOTHING IN THIS CHAPTER CHANGES v1.

Your v1 rules remain exactly as documented in Chapters 10–21. These are proposals to evaluate after you have at least 50 (better 100) journaled v1 trades. Adopt any change explicitly, give it a version number (v1.1, v2.0) and log it in the Change Log.

# Proposal Rationale / evidence Trade-off How to test
1 Clarify VWAP Length — use a true session VWAP (or Anchored VWAP at 9:30) if your test shows Length 14 creates a rolling VWAP Session VWAP is the standard institutional benchmark that the “price above VWAP” thesis assumes A rolling VWAP reacts faster, which some may prefer Run the Chapter 3 test; compare alert hit-rates for 2 weeks
2 ATR guard-rails on the stop — skip if stop distance < 0.3 ATR (too tight) or > 1.5–2 ATR (too wide) Makes “unacceptable risk” objective Fewer trades Journal: compare R results by stop/ATR bucket
3 Market regime filter — LONG only if SPY 5m Close > VWAP; SHORT only if below Most stocks move with the index Fewer counter-trend winners Tag “market regime” in journal; compare
4 Formal ranking score (Chapter 15 rubric) Removes subjective picking Effort Correlate score with R result after 50 trades
5 No new entries in the last 30 minutes Closing flows, RVOL distortion, less time to reach 2R Fewer trades Journal by time of day
6 Stop-limit entries with a cap (e.g., limit = trigger + 0.2R) Prevents terrible fills Some missed fills. Not available in the TrendSpider widget [TS]; would require Alpaca directly Compare slippage
7 Partial at +1R, stop to break-even Smooths the equity curve Lowers average winner Needs 100+ trades; cannot be Strategy-Tested [TS]
8 Earnings and SSR exclusion in the scanner Earnings and SSR change behaviour Fewer candidates The scanner supports earnings conditions [TS]
9 Exit C refinement — require both VWAP close-through and EMA cross, or 2 consecutive closes Fewer premature exits Larger losses on true failures Simulate from journal screenshots
10 Time-of-day RVOL (volume vs same time on prior days) Removes open/close distortion May need a custom indicator Verify TrendSpider options
11 Daily loss limit and max positions adopted as hard rules Behavioural protection None meaningful Adopt directly
